slides.title: What Is Polymorphism?
slides.content: Polymorphism means 'many forms.' In C#, it allows a base class reference to point to objects of different derived types, and when you call a virtual method, the correct derived version runs based on the actual object type—selected at runtime (dynamic dispatch).

options: Calling the same method name on different object types with different behavior
Hiding all methods in a class
exercise.answer: Calling the same method name on different object types with different behavior

slides.title: Virtual Methods
slides.content: A 'virtual' method in a base class provides a default implementation that derived classes can replace. The base method must be marked 'virtual' for it to be overridden. When called through a base reference, the runtime decides which implementation to run.

exercise.prompt: Mark this method as overridable in derived classes: 'public _____ void Fly() { }'

slides.title: Override Keyword
slides.content: The 'override' keyword in a derived class method replaces the implementation of a virtual method from the base class. It must have the same signature (name, parameters, return type) and the method it overrides must be virtual, abstract, or itself an override.

exercise.prompt: Override the Greet method in the Student class to print 'Hello, I am a student'.
hints: Make sure your code includes the required keywords/elements: class, virtual, public
When run, your code should output: Hello, I am a student

slides.title: Base Class References and Runtime Dispatch
slides.content: When you call a virtual method through a base class reference, the runtime uses the actual object's type to decide which method to call. This is the heart of polymorphism—the most derived override always wins, regardless of the reference type.
slides.example:
Animal a = new Dog();  // base ref, derived object
a.Speak();  // Calls Dog.Speak(), not Animal.Speak()

a = new Cat();
a.Speak();  // Now calls Cat.Speak()

exercise.prompt: Animal a = new Dog(); a.Speak(); — if Speak is virtual+override, which version runs?

slides.title: Method Hiding with 'new'
slides.content: If a derived class defines a method with the same name and signature as a non-virtual base method, it hides the base method. Use 'new' to explicitly indicate hiding. Unlike override, this is resolved at compile-time by the reference type, not the object type.

exercise.prompt: Which keyword is used to hide (not override) a base class method?

slides.title: Abstract Methods and Classes
slides.content: An abstract method has no implementation in the base class—it is just a signature. The base class must be 'abstract'. Derived classes MUST override abstract methods. This enforces a contract that all derived classes implement the method.

exercise.prompt: An abstract class _____ be instantiated directly.

slides.title: The base Keyword in Overrides
slides.content: Inside an override, you can call the base class's virtual implementation using 'base.Method()'. This lets you extend the base behavior rather than completely replacing it—useful for chaining behavior in a hierarchy.

exercise.prompt: In the override, call the base class implementation first, then add extra behavior.
hints: Make sure your code includes the required keywords/elements: base, Greet
When run, your code should output: Hello, ---

slides.title: Polymorphism in Collections
slides.content: Polymorphism shines when processing collections of related objects. You can store different derived types in a single array or list of the base type, then iterate and call virtual methods—the correct override runs for each object.

exercise.prompt: When iterating a List<Animal> containing Dogs and Cats with a virtual MakeSound, what happens?
options: Each object calls its own overridden MakeSound
exercise.answer: Each object calls its own overridden MakeSound
